title: Elementary functions and logarithms: the platform libm per type; logs divide
verdict: fp64 as the libm (tan 2.3 ulp on macOS); `log10`, `log(b)` 1.5 to 2.1 ulp; `Float32` in single precision, `log()` 1.5 ulp
description: Each function is Rust's `f64` or `f32` method, so `Float64` calls the libm's double function and `Float32` its float one (`sinf`, `expf`, …) and returns `Float32` (polars-elem-rounding). `sqrt` is the hardware instruction, correctly rounded. `log(base)` is Rust's `x.log(base)`, `ln(x) / ln(base)` in the column's type (polars-log-base, PL-4); `log10()` is `log(10)`, and there is no `log2`, so `log(2)` serves. For `Float64` the default base `e` rounds to a double whose `ln` is 1.0, so `log()` is `ln`.

Max error in ulps, measured on macOS arm64 (3 000 inputs each), fp64 / fp32: sqrt 0.5 / 0.5; exp 0.502 / 0.511; log() 0.500 / 1.500 (528 of 746 fp32 results off, PL-4); log10() 2.09 / 1.53; log(2) 1.46 / 1.15; log(3) 2.05 / 1.53; log(b) with a column base 2.13 / 1.63; `**` with a column exponent (powf) 0.504 / 0.510; sin 0.77 / 0.77; cos 0.83 / 0.72; tan 2.30 / 0.63; arcsin 0.61 / 0.63; arccos 0.89 / 0.63; arctan 0.72 / 0.65; arctan2 0.56 / 0.68.

The fp64 functions return the same values as DuckDB's on every probed input (same libm). Unlike DuckDB, `log10` and `log(2)` divide two logarithms where DuckDB calls `log10` and `log2` (≤ 0.502 ulp), and `Float32` computes in single precision where DuckDB widens to double: the macOS float functions stay below 0.8 ulp but miss the correctly rounded value up to 30 % of the time (arctan 893 of 3 000).

Linux x86_64 (glibc, version unknown; the glibc 2.39 manual's bounds): double exp, log, sin, cos, asin, acos, atan, pow 1 ulp, tan and atan2 no known error; float expf, logf, sinf, cosf, tanf, asinf, acosf, atanf, powf 1 ulp, atan2f 2 ulp. Polars's `log10` and `log(b)` add about 1.5 ulp to the libm's `log` error by their formula. To be measured on homelab.
reference: The reference computes these with Lean's `Float` (the platform's libm, in double) and fixes `rounding: TIE_TO_EVEN`; the last bits are each engine's (#54). sverify's ε (#85) per function, type and platform comes from this table; `Float32` would round to binary32 in the reference.

evidence.note: Float32 and Float64 each call the generic body: f32 or f64 methods
log(base): x.log(base) in the column's float type
a non-integer or column exponent: Pow::pow (powf)
f64::log: 'may not be correctly rounded', ln(self) / ln(base)

glibc 2.39 manual, table 'Known Maximum Errors in Math Functions', x86_64 column, in ulps: double acos 1, asin 1, atan 1, atan2 -, cos 1, exp 1, log 1, log10 2, log2 2, pow 1, sin 1, sqrt -, tan -; float acosf 1, asinf 1, atanf 1, atan2f 2, cosf 1, expf 1, logf 1, log10f 2, log2f 1, powf 1, sinf 1, sqrtf -, tanf 1. '-' is no known error beyond correct rounding.

The current manual drops the table: glibc aims at results 'within a few ulp' and correct rounding only for sqrt, fma, rint and string conversions; its test suite flags errors above 9 ulp. The numbers are the largest errors glibc's tests have found, not proved bounds.

provenance.notes: For the Linux x86_64 column. The glibc version on a given Linux machine is unknown here (`ldd --version` gives it); the 2.39 table is the last that lists x86_64. macOS's libm documents no error bounds (the SDK's man pages for sin, tan, log, pow state special values only), so the macOS column rests on the probe.

notes: Probe script ulp_probe.py (session scratchpad, not in the repository), run from python/ as `uv run --with mpmath python ulp_probe.py --n 3000 --seed 1 --out ulp.json`: about 3 000 inputs per operation and type, random and hard cases, against mpmath at 256 bits. 'bad' counts results that differ from the correctly rounded value; the max is in ulps of the result type at the exact value's binade. DuckDB runs on a table loaded from Parquet, Polars on a LazyFrame with collect(engine='streaming'), so the column kernels run. DuckDB 2.0.0 and Polars 2.1.0 (Python wheels), macOS 26.6 arm64, Python 3.12.11, mpmath 1.3.0.

Elementwise kernels are shared by the streaming and in-memory engines (polars-elem-rounding, polars-double-scalar-divisor); the probe collects with engine='streaming' on 3 000-row frames, so morsels hold more than one row and the literal paths run.
